items.body:
The e2e test framework has several patterns that cause flakiness, silent resource leaks, and hard-to-debug failures, especially in disruptive tests that restart API servers or control plane components. PR 137832 addresses these across 13 files (185 additions, 41 deletions), touching SIG api-machinery, apps, cloud-provider, network, node, storage, and testing.

Error suppression hides resource leaks. Across the test suite, cleanup code discards errors from Delete calls. In test/e2e/apimachinery/aggregator.go, the cleanupSampleAPIServer function has 10 such calls (APIService, Deployment, Secret, Service, ServiceAccount, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding, ClusterRole) all silently swallowed. Same pattern in test/e2e/apimachinery/apply.go (4 deployments/pods), test/e2e/apps/rc.go (DeleteCollection), and test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go (ConfigMaps in defer blocks). When these fail, resources leak into subsequent tests with zero trace of what went wrong.

No retry on transient API server errors. GetControlPlaneNodes in test/e2e/framework/util.go calls Nodes().List() and immediately fails on any error. During disruptive tests (daemon restarts, etcd failure injection), the API server is expected to be briefly unreachable. The same issue exists in allNodesReady at test/e2e/framework/node/helper.go and RestartNodes at test/e2e/common/util.go. A transient connection refused or 503 kills the entire test instead of retrying. The fix introduces IsRetryableAPIError which checks for connection refused/reset, server timeout, 429, 503, 500, and unexpected server errors, plus a new WaitForControlPlaneNodes that wraps the listing in a polling loop with retry-on-transient logic.

Healthz returns 200 before daemon is ready. RestartDaemonConfig.waitUp in test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go considers the daemon ready when /healthz returns HTTP 200. After a kubelet restart, the health endpoint can report ok while kubelet is still recovering. Logs show errors, pods are not yet scheduled. The fix adds verifyDaemonReadiness which SSHes into the node and checks the last 20 lines of /var/log/kubelet.log for error patterns before declaring readiness.

Goroutines not gracefully stopped. In test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go, a cache.NewInformer controller is started with go controller.Run(backgroundCtx.Done()). The cleanup calls cancel() but does not wait for the controller goroutine to finish. The fix replaces this with a dedicated stopCh channel and DeferCleanup that closes the channel then sleeps 100ms to allow graceful shutdown.

PVC deletion races with pod references. DeleteAllStatefulSets in test/e2e/framework/statefulset/rest.go has a TODO comment about not checking whether pods still reference PVCs before deleting them. The current code deletes PVCs immediately, which can fail or leave orphaned PVs when pods are still running. The fix lists pods, checks volume references, and only deletes PVCs that are not in use, with foreground propagation.

Duplicated control plane filtering. GetControlPlaneNodes and WaitForControlPlaneNodes both contain the same node filtering logic (check for control-plane label and NoSchedule taint). The second commit extracts this into a shared filterControlPlaneNodes helper.

All changes are in e2e test code, no user-facing impact.

Related issues:
- 109600: prevent the Expect(err).NotTo(HaveOccurred()) and ExpectNoError(err) anti-pattern in e2e tests (same category of error handling problems)
- 86253: sample-apiserver returns error instead of falling back to second Accept type (directly affects the aggregator.go test modified in this PR)
- 135285: GOAWAY are not handled gracefully in apiserver when aggregating (related network error handling)
- 105536: Orphaned pod found, but error not a directory occurred when trying to remove the volumes dir (related resource cleanup issue)

items.body:
### What happened?

Using [FormatAndMount](https://github.com/kubernetes/mount-utils/blob/d06d436a17294305776494aa876d6e8e38c9200c/mount.go#L189) library from kubernetes/mount-utils ends in re-formatting partially broken filesystem instead of failing erroring out. 

### What did you expect to happen?

If filesystem is partially broken (i.e primary superblock of filesystem got corrupted) instead of silently re-formatting the device library should error out.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

It will be tricky to reproduce issue, but I will list steps:

Incident timeline: how a killed  fsck  leads to data loss

• **T0 — Initial provisioning**: The application (pod) is scheduled onto the node for the first time. During the  NodeStageVolume  request, the CSI driver formats the disk with a filesystem (ext4) and mounts it.
• **T1 — Data written, then there is reboot of node**: The application writes a significant amount of data. Before this data is fully flushed to disk, the node restarts unexpectedly, leaving the filesystem in a dirty (inconsistent) state.
• **T2 — Re-stage triggers fsck**: The node comes back online and the pod is rescheduled. The CSI node driver receives a fresh  NodeStageVolume  request for the same volume. Because it uses mount-utils'  FormatAndMount , it detects an existing filesystem and unconditionally runs  fsck  to repair it.
• **T3 — fsck killed mid-repair**: While  fsck  is still running, the node restarts again (or the  fsck  process is killed). Interrupting  fsck  mid-write can corrupt the filesystem's primary superblock.
• **T4 — Silent reformat wipes data**: The node comes back online and the driver receives another  NodeStageVolume  request. This time, the filesystem check reports no filesystem (because  blkid  can only read the now-corrupted primary superblock). Treating the disk as unformatted,  FormatAndMount  reformats it as ext4 — wiping all previously written data, even though the data was still recoverable via backup superblocks.

items.body:
#### Which jobs are flaking?

pull-kubernetes-unit (top job in the k8s-metrics flake feed for this package; 3 jobs total)

#### Which tests are flaking?

`Test_UncertainDeviceGlobalMounts` and `Test_UncertainVolumeMountState` in `pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler`, with occasional knock-on failures in other tests of the same package.

#### Since when has it been flaking?

At least the week of 2026-07-06: 9 failures across 3 jobs for `k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager reconciler` in the flake feed.

#### Reason for failure (if possible)

Both tests run their table cases as parallel subtests, and each subtest starts a reconciler goroutine (`reconciler.Run`) with a stop channel that is never closed. Every finished subtest therefore leaks a reconciler that keeps spinning at the test's 1ns loop interval. The leaked reconcilers starve the remaining subtests; under load their wait helpers exceed the ~36s exponential backoff budget and fail with:

```
reconciler_test.go: Timed out waiting for volume "fake-plugin/timeout-setup-volume" to be detached.
```

Reproducible locally with:

```
go test ./pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler -race -count=30 -timeout=45m
```

On an otherwise idle 16-core machine this failed `Test_UncertainVolumeMountState` in 7 of 30 runs and `Test_UncertainDeviceGlobalMounts` in 2 of 30, plus knock-on failures in `Test_Run_Positive_VolumeFSResizeControllerAttachEnabled` and `Test_Run_Positive_VolumeUnmapControllerAttachEnabled`, and the leak roughly triples the package runtime by the later iterations.

#### Anything else we need to know?

Fix is straightforward: stop each reconciler when its subtest returns (the pattern `Test_Run_Positive_VolumeFSResizeControllerAttachEnabled` already uses) and create the ktesting context per subtest. PR to follow.

items.body:
## What happens

On kubelet start/restart (node reboot, kubelet upgrade, cold node join), pods that mount secret
or configMap volumes intermittently fail to mount with a `FailedMount` event:

```
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "sec" : object "bootrace-min"/"s37" not registered
```

It is transient and clears on the volume reconciler's next pass, but delays pod startup and
generates many `FailedMount` events at scale (node reboots, node-pool upgrades).

## Environment

- Kubernetes: reproduced on v1.31.14; symptom reported across 1.22–1.27 (see related issues).
- Node: 2 vCPU Linux, containerd, single-node kubeadm cluster.

## Reproduce

Small node (e.g. **2 vCPU**), kubelet `maxPods` raised to fit the pod count: create N pods each
mounting its **own distinct** secret + configMap, then restart kubelet a few times. A *shared*
object does not reproduce; the objects must be distinct.

```bash
./repro.sh                 # 150 distinct-object pods, 6 kubelet restarts (defaults)
```

<details>
<summary>repro.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# USAGE: ./repro.sh [NUM_PODS] [RESTARTS] [SETTLE_SECS]   (defaults: 150 6 25)
# ENV:   NS, NODE, RESTART_CMD="sudo systemctl restart kubelet"
# Requires kubectl + ability to restart kubelet on the node. Raise kubelet maxPods to fit NUM_PODS.
set -uo pipefail
N="${1:-150}"; R="${2:-6}"; SETTLE="${3:-25}"
NS="${NS:-bootrace-min}"
RESTART_CMD="${RESTART_CMD:-sudo systemctl restart kubelet}"
NODE="${NODE:-$(kubectl get nodes --no-headers 2>/dev/null | awk '$2=="Ready"{print $1; exit}')}"
[ -z "$NODE" ] && { echo "ERROR: no Ready node; set NODE=<name>"; exit 1; }

kubectl create namespace "$NS" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: Secret\nmetadata: {name: s%d, namespace: %s}\nstringData: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: ConfigMap\nmetadata: {name: c%d, namespace: %s}\ndata: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do cat <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: p$i, namespace: $NS, labels: {app: bootrace-min}}
spec:
  nodeName: $NODE
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
  tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: sec, mountPath: /etc/sec, readOnly: true}
    - {name: cm,  mountPath: /etc/cm,  readOnly: true}
  volumes:
  - {name: sec, secret: {secretName: s$i}}
  - {name: cm,  configMap: {name: c$i}}
---
EOF
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null

for t in $(seq 1 120); do
  run=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Running --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
  [ "$run" -ge "$N" ] && break; sleep 4
done
echo "Running: $run / $N"

total=0
for b in $(seq 1 "$R"); do
  kubectl -n "$NS" delete events --all >/dev/null 2>&1
  eval "$RESTART_CMD"
  sleep "$SETTLE"
  hits=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get events --field-selector reason=FailedMount \
           -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.message}{"\n"}{end}' 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'not registered')
  total=$((total + hits))
  printf 'restart %2d/%d | FailedMount "not registered": %d\n' "$b" "$R" "$hits"
done
echo "TOTAL 'not registered' FailedMount events: $total"
echo "Cleanup: kubectl delete ns $NS"
```
</details>

### Sample output (single-node, 2 vCPU, 150 distinct-object pods)

```
restart  1/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 14
restart  2/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 4
restart  3/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 58
restart  4/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 46
restart  5/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 15
restart  6/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 6
TOTAL 'not registered' FailedMount events: 143
```

Inspect: `kubectl -n bootrace-min get events --field-selector reason=FailedMount | grep 'not registered'`

- #119361 — Sporadic "MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ... not registered" (1.27)

items.body:
### What happened?

Volume populators (e.g. [hello-populator](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/lib-volume-populator/tree/master/example/hello-populator)) create a temporary "prime" PVC, provision and populate a PV through it, then rebind the PV to the original PVC. After the rebind, the prime PVC always receives a `Warning ClaimMisbound "Two claims are bound to the same volume, this one is bound incorrectly"` event. This is a false positive — the rebind is the designed and expected flow, not an error condition.

The `Lost` phase transition on the prime PVC is correct and necessary (lib-volume-populator polls for it as confirmation that the rebind succeeded), but the warning event creates noise for users and monitoring systems on every populator operation.

### What did you expect to happen?

The PV controller should recognize that a deliberate populator rebind is not an error condition. The prime PVC should still transition to `Lost`, but the event should be downgraded to `Normal` with an appropriate message (e.g. `Normal ClaimLost "Claim is being replaced by a volume populator and is no longer needed"`).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy the [hello-populator](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/lib-volume-populator/tree/master/example/hello-populator) example volume populator
2. Create a `Hello` CR and a PVC with a `dataSourceRef` pointing to it
3. Wait for population to complete and the PV to be rebound to the original PVC
4. Observe the `Warning ClaimMisbound` event on the prime PVC

This happens on every populator operation, 100% of the time.

### Anything else we need to know?

This affects any volume populator built on lib-volume-populator (hello-populator, CDI, etc.). It was observed in practice as a contributing factor in kubevirt/kubevirt#17724, where `ClaimMisbound` events during volume migration added confusion when debugging and triggered false alerts.

`spec.volumeName` is immutable once set, so the populator cannot clear it on the prime PVC before rebinding — the only fix is on the PV controller side.

items.body:
### What happened?

After upgrading a Talos Kubernetes cluster from v1.35 to v1.36, some running pods stopped receiving projected service account token rotations. The affected pods were not terminating.

During the control-plane restart window, kubelet logged transient TokenRequest / NodeAuthorizer failures like:

`Error preparing data for projected volume sa-token for pod network/external-5f8b6fdd5c-g4vzm: failed to fetch token: serviceaccounts "external" is forbidden: User "system:node:k8s-1" cannot create resource "serviceaccounts/token" in API group "" in the namespace "network": no relationship found between node 'k8s-1' and this object`

There were also kubelet TokenRequest EOFs against the local API endpoint:

`Couldn't update token: Post "https://127.0.0.1:7445/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/serviceaccounts/default/token": EOF`

After the API server became healthy again, the projected token files stayed stale for hours. Example affected pod:

pod: network/external-5f8b6fdd5c-g4vzm
node: k8s-1
token iat: 2026-04-28T20:46:41Z
token exp: 2026-04-28T21:46:41Z
projected volume symlink stayed at: ..2026_04_28_20_46_41...

A second pod on another node had a token issued at 2026-04-28T20:52:02Z, expiring at 2026-04-28T21:52:02Z, and also remained frozen at that timestamp.

The application impact was Envoy Gateway data-plane pods failing xDS authentication after token expiry:

`failed to validate token {"error": "token review found error: [invalid bearer token, service account token has expired]"}`

Because the Envoy data-plane could not reconnect to xDS, it kept stale endpoint config until the pods were restarted.


### What did you expect to happen?

For running pods, kubelet should keep retrying projected service account token refresh after transient TokenRequest/API server/NodeAuthorizer failures.

A temporary failure during apiserver restart should not leave the projected token file permanently stale or expired. Once the apiserver/NodeAuthorizer state is healthy again, kubelet should recover token rotation without
requiring the pod to be restarted.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I do not yet have a minimal deterministic reproducer, but the observed incident was:

1. Run a pod with a projected service account token, for example expirationSeconds: 3600.
2. Restart or upgrade the control plane while kubelet is refreshing projected tokens.
3. During the restart, kubelet receives TokenRequest failures such as:
   serviceaccounts "<name>" is forbidden ... no relationship found between node '<node>' and this object
   or EOFs from the API endpoint.
4. Wait past the projected token expiration.
5. Inspect the projected token file/symlink inside the pod or from the host.
6. Observe that the token remains expired and the projected volume timestamp does not advance, even after the API server is healthy again.
7. Restarting the pod causes a fresh token to be mounted and resolves the issue.


### Anything else we need to know?

This does not appear to be an application-level token caching issue. In the observed case, Envoy’s SDS secret last-updated timestamp matched the projected token file timestamp. The file itself stopped changing.

This also seems different from:

- #116481, which involves terminating pods/preStop hooks.
- #130442, which involved PVCs in terminating state.

The affected pods here were ordinary running pods.

items.body:
**CVSS Rating:**  
[CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3-1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H) — **Medium (6.5)**

A vulnerability was discovered in the Kubernetes CSI Driver for SMB where the subDir parameter in volume identifiers was insufficiently validated. Attackers with the ability to create PersistentVolumes referencing the SMB CSI driver could craft volume identifiers containing path traversal sequences (../). During volume deletion or cleanup operations, the driver could operate on unintended directories outside the intended managed path within the SMB export.

This may lead to deletion or modification of directories on the SMB server.

### Am I vulnerable?

You may be vulnerable if:
You run the CSI Driver for SMB (smb.csi.k8s.io)
Your cluster allows users to create PersistentVolumes referencing the SMB CSI driver
Your CSI driver version does not validate traversal sequences in the subDir field


#### Affected Versions
All versions of the CSI Driver for SMB prior to the v1.20.1 release containing the fix for traversal validation are affected.

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

This issue can be mitigated by:
Upgrading the CSI Driver for SMB to a patched version
Restricting PersistentVolume creation privileges to trusted administrators
Reviewing SMB exports to ensure only intended directories are writable by the driver

As a best practice, untrusted users should not be granted permission to create arbitrary PersistentVolumes referencing external storage drivers.


#### Fixed Versions

CSI Driver for SMB versions >= v1.20.1

### Detection

To determine if your cluster may be affected:
Inspect PersistentVolumes using the SMB CSI driver and review the volumeHandle field.
Look for traversal sequences such as: `../`
Review CSI controller logs for unexpected directory operations. e.g. “Removing subPath: /tmp/mount-uuid/legitimate/../../../exports/subdir”

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by @Shaul Ben Hai, Senior Staff Security Researcher from SentinelOne.

The issue was fixed by the CSI Driver for SMB maintainers and the Kubernetes Security Response Committee.

items.body:
#### What would you like to be added / why is this needed?

Refactor `pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go` so directory setup and medium-specific mounts are layered clearly, and add focused tests for behavior that was only covered indirectly.

**Problem**

- `setupTmpfs` and `setupHugepages` implicitly required `setupDir` to run first, but the call pattern was inconsistent: for default medium, `setupDir` ran directly; for memory-backed and hugepages volumes, `setupTmpfs` / `setupHugepages` called `setupDir` internally. That mixed “mount” helpers with directory creation and made responsibilities unclear.
- `setupDir` had no dedicated unit tests for its permission checks and `chmod` correction logic.

**Proposed approach**

- Always create the directory in `SetUpAt` first, then run the medium-specific mount (`setupTmpfs` / `setupHugepages`) without those functions calling `setupDir` internally.
- Add `os.Stat` preconditions in `setupTmpfs` and `setupHugepages` so missing directories fail fast with clear errors (extra `stat` is O(1) and negligible vs existing `MkdirAll` / mount work).

**Tests (tracked in PR)**

- Extend `TestSetupHugepages` for the new `os.Stat` guard.
- Add `TestSetupTmpfs` for the guard, nil mounter, mount detector errors, and the already-mounted memory case (idempotent path).
- Add `TestSetupDir` for permission verification and `os.Chmod` correction.

**User-facing impact**

None — cleanup / test coverage only.

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: sig/storage

items.body:
## What happened?

`DetachBlockISCSIDisk` in `pkg/volume/iscsi/iscsi_util.go` does not call `deleteDevices` to clean up SCSI device entries and flush multipath device maps after detaching a block iSCSI volume.

The parallel function `DetachDisk` (for filesystem iSCSI volumes) correctly calls `deleteDevices` at line 632 before locking the target and logging out. `DetachBlockISCSIDisk` skips this step entirely.

## What did you expect to happen?

Both detach paths should clean up SCSI devices and multipath maps. After detaching a block iSCSI volume, `/dev/sdX` entries and multipath device maps should be removed from the node, matching the behavior of filesystem volume detach.

## How can we reproduce it?

1. Attach a block iSCSI volume to a node (with multipath configured)
2. Detach the volume
3. Observe that `/dev/sdX` entries and multipath maps remain on the node

Compare with filesystem iSCSI volume detach, which correctly cleans up both.

## Anything else we need to know?

The issue is a missing call in `DetachBlockISCSIDisk`. The cleanup logic is in `deleteDevices` which currently only accepts `iscsiDiskUnmounter` (filesystem type). Both `iscsiDiskUnmounter` and `iscsiDiskUnmapper` (block type) have the required fields (`iscsiDisk`, `exec`, `deviceUtil`), so the fix is to extract the cleanup logic into a shared function callable from both paths.

/kind bug

```diff
        cmd := exec.Command(quotaCmd, "-t", mountsFile, "-P/dev/null", "-D/dev/null", "-x", "-f", mountpoint, "-c", command)

-       data, err := cmd.Output()
+       data, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()
+       klog.V(4).Infof("runXFSQuotaCommand output:\n%s", string(data))
        if err != nil {
                return "", err
        }
-       klog.V(4).Infof("runXFSQuotaCommand output %q", string(data))
        return string(data), nil
 }
```
The relevant kubelet logs are as follows:
```text
Mar 17 21:58:08 ubuntu24-test kubelet[2984]: I0317 21:58:08.149043    2984 quota_common_linux_impl.go:131] runXFSQuotaCommand /sbin/xfs_quota -t /tmp/mounts1038897217 -P/dev/null -D/dev/null -x -f /var/lib/kubelet -c project -s -p /var/lib/kubelet/pods/91fd6e02-f0b4-45c6-a328-0fba789f2da6/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/test-storage 1048579
```

items.body:
**CVSS Rating:**  
[CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3-1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H) — **Medium (6.5)**

A vulnerability was discovered in the Kubernetes CSI Driver for NFS where the subDir parameter in volume identifiers was insufficiently validated. Attackers with the ability to create PersistentVolumes referencing the NFS CSI driver could craft volume identifiers containing path traversal sequences (../). During volume deletion or cleanup operations, the driver could operate on unintended directories outside the intended managed path within the NFS export.

This may lead to deletion or modification of directories on the NFS server.

### Am I vulnerable?

You may be vulnerable if:
You run the CSI Driver for NFS (nfs.csi.k8s.io)
Your cluster allows users to create PersistentVolumes referencing the NFS CSI driver
Your CSI driver version does not validate traversal sequences in the subDir field


#### Affected Versions
All versions of the CSI Driver for NFS prior to the v4.13.1 release containing the fix for traversal validation are affected.

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

This issue can be mitigated by:
Upgrading the CSI Driver for NFS to a patched version
Restricting PersistentVolume creation privileges to trusted administrators
Reviewing NFS exports to ensure only intended directories are writable by the driver

As a best practice, untrusted users should not be granted permission to create arbitrary PersistentVolumes referencing external storage drivers.


#### Fixed Versions

CSI Driver for NFS versions >= v4.13.1

### Detection

To determine if your cluster may be affected:
Inspect PersistentVolumes using the NFS CSI driver and review the volumeHandle field.
Look for traversal sequences such as: `../`
Review CSI controller logs for unexpected directory operations. e.g. “Removing subPath: /tmp/mount-uuid/legitimate/../../../exports/subdir”

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by Shaul Ben Hai, Senior Staff Security Researcher from SentinelOne.

The issue was fixed by the CSI Driver for NFS maintainers and the Kubernetes Security Response Committee.

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
### What happened?

When creating a pod with a projected `serviceAccountToken` volume and all containers have the same `runAsUser`, kubelet configure the file owner UID of the token file to the the `runAsUser`.

However, the existing implementation only sets the file owner of file in the timestamped directory. The link file is still owned by root. This is because `pkg/volume/util/atomic_writer_linux.go#chown` makes use of `os.Chown()`, which applies changes to the link's target instead of the link file itself.

We can use `os.Lchown()` to configure owner UID of the link file properly.

```
$ ls -lA
total 0
drwxr-xr-x    2 root     root            60 Mar  1 19:17 ..2026_03_01_19_17_08.1191223127
lrwxrwxrwx    1 root     root            32 Mar  1 19:17 ..data -> ..2026_03_01_19_17_08.1191223127
lrwxrwxrwx    1 root     root            12 Mar  1 19:17 token -> ..data/token

$ ls -lA ..2026_03_01_19_17_08.1191223127/
total 4
-rw-------    1 1000     root          1089 Mar  1 19:17 token

$ ls -lA ..data/
total 4
-rw-------    1 1000     root          1089 Mar  1 19:17 token
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Both the file in the timestamped directory and the link file should be owned by `runAsUser`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
kind: Pod
metadata:
```

items.title: Remove / deprecate the `csi.volume.kubernetes.io/nodeid` annotation of the Node object?

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: lifecycle/rotten
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR that has aged beyond stale and will be auto-closed.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
This annotation `csi.volume.kubernetes.io/nodeid` was used internally to specify the identifier for a node as understood by the Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver. kubelet [populated this annotation](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/csi/nodeinfomanager/nodeinfomanager.go#L118) by calling the `NodeGetInfo` gRPC method of the CSI driver to retrieve the node ID during the driver registration process. The external-attacher sidecar container [read this annotation](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-attacher/pull/213) to get the node ID when attaching or detaching volumes.

But it should be deprecated in favor of the `CSINode` object, which provides the same functionality via the `spec.drivers[].nodeID` field. And it needs the csi driver to bump the external-attacher sidecar to v2.2 or later. See [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-attacher/blob/cc32e8cebcb4433b84c26aacc59e200aecd9f5be/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-2.2.md?plain=1#L11) for details.

According to [the external-attacher documentation](https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/external-attacher.html), v2.2 is out of support. So all the third-party CSI drivers should upgrade the external-attacher sidecar container to v4.6.1 or a later version, which does not rely on the deprecated annotation anymore.

The [old design proposal](https://github.com/kubernetes/design-proposals-archive/blob/main/storage/container-storage-interface.md) indicates that this annotation is deprecated and will be removed according to deprecation policy (1 year after deprecation) with a TODO item (mark deprecation date).

Can we mark the "stable" annotation `csi.volume.kubernetes.io/nodeid` as deprecated in 1.36 and remove it in 1.40 (or 1 year after the deprecation)?

- https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy/
- https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/54035 document the deprecation of this annotation.

If removal is planned, should we automatically remove the annotation from the existing Node objects when kubelet stops populating it?

/sig node
/sig storage
/cc @jsafrane @dims @liggitt

items.body:
## Summary

Remove the last remaining reference to the deprecated `wait.NewExponentialBackoffManager` function from the codebase, located in `pkg/volume/csi/csi_attacher.go`.

## Background

As part of the effort to remove the deprecated `wait.NewExponentialBackoffManager` API (see #136823), PRs #136824 and #137066 have already migrated other usages. The only remaining reference is in `csi_attacher.go:495`.

## Migration Pattern

Per the deprecation notice and the approach used in #136824, replace:

```go
backoffMgr := wait.NewExponentialBackoffManager(initBackoff, maxBackoff, resetDuration, backoffFactor, jitter, clock)

for {
    t := backoffMgr.Backoff()
    select {
    case <-t.C():
        // do work
    case <-ctx.Done():
        t.Stop()
        // handle timeout
    }
}
```

With:

```go
delayFunc := wait.Backoff{
    Duration: initBackoff,
    Cap:      maxBackoff,
    Steps:    math.MaxInt32,
    Factor:   backoffFactor,
    Jitter:   jitter,
}.DelayWithReset(clk, resetDuration)

for {
    select {
    case <-clk.After(delayFunc()):
        // do work
    case <-ctx.Done():
        // handle timeout
    }
}
```

## Location

- File: `pkg/volume/csi/csi_attacher.go`
- Function: `waitForVolumeAttachDetachStatusWithLister`
- Line: 495

### What would you like to be added?

This is a feature request for Kubernetes to resize memory-backed volumes without container restarts, similar to in-place pod resizing for CPU / memory.

### Why is this needed?

Ray project is working on an integration to use kuebrnetes in-place pod resizing in the Ray autoscaler. When upsizing memory in-place, we need to also resize the memory backed volume Ray uses for it's object store. This object store is typically configured to use ~30% of the memory requests in the Pod. Ray autoscaler can be responsible for setting the size but needs the ability to resize memory-backed volumes without restarts.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Some CSI drivers (e.g. https://github.com/outscale/osc-bsu-csi-driver up to v1.7.0) support OFFLINE volume expansion only. If the users would like to resize PVC for pods controlled by StatefulSet, they should manually scale down all replicas before the external-resizer controller can resize the volumes. Otherwise, the StatefulSet controller creates the new Pod immediately without giving a chance for the _AttachDetachController_ to detach the volume from the worker.

It would be good to support OFFLINE volume expansion using the StatfulSet rolling upgrade strategy.

### Why is this needed?

Deployments with CSI drivers that support OFFLINE volume resize can still benefit from application no-downtime using a StatefulSet rolling upgrade strategy.

items.body:
Is it possible to extend `CSIStorageCapacity` tracking so that the scheduler also considers it when scheduling pods whose PVCs are already bound?

When a node hosting a pod is drained (for example, during maintenance or upgrades), the pod needs to be rescheduled. Currently, the scheduler does not use `CSIStorageCapacity` information for pods with bound PVCs. For storage backends that support volume rebuild or migration, it would be useful if the scheduler could prefer nodes with sufficient available storage capacity, so that the new node can accommodate the original volume and keep the pod and volume co-located for better I/O performance. At the moment, this is not supported, and pods can occasionally be scheduled onto nodes where volumes cannot be rebuilt.

Do you think this should be addressed on the Kubernetes side, or does it need to be handled by the storage backend? If on the Kubernetes side, this could potentially be implemented by adding a new field to StorageClass.

/sig storage
/sig scheduling

### What happened?

During the process of attaching volumes by kubelet, if the CSI plugin is not registered, it will only be known whether the CSI plugin is registered when the kubelet actually calls the CSI's volume mount method (SetUp). If the CSI plugin is not registered and there are too many volumes to mount, this can cause the kubelet CPU usage to spike in a short period of time.
Should we check whether the CSI plugin is registered before mounting the volume? This could reduce unnecessary coroutine creation and lower CPU usage.
The CSI plugin is only checked for existence when the SetUpAt method is called.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2a3a6605ac9b184711ef212ecbe26c8af4a8bac8/pkg/volume/csi/csi_mounter.go#L102-L110

After kubelet knows whether CSI is registered, it proceeds with volume mounting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A node has multiple pods, and there are a large number of volumes that need to be mounted by CSI. However, the CSI plugin is not registered.

items.body:
### What happened?

/sig scheduling

I was verifying a scenario where two pods with topology spread and PVCs with WaitForFirstConsumer storage got their PVCs assigned to the same node, resulting in one of the pods becoming unschedulable due to conflicting rules (topology spread prevents using the same node, volume binding enforces using that node).

The suspected root cause was a pod binding failure or scheduler restart, something like:

1. Pod#1's PVC is bound to Node#1
2. Pod#1 fails to bind
3. Pod#2's PVC is bound to Node#1
4. Pod#2 is bound to Node#1
5. Pod#1 is unschedulable because it has to use Node#1 due to the PVC binding but can't use it due to pod topology spread

I wrote an integration test to repro, and it's still reproducible even with the `NominatedNodeNameForExpectation` feature enabled.

Upon further investigation, it seems that the NominatedNodeName is cleared on binding error, so scheduler isn't aware of Pod#1 initial assignment when scheduling Pod#2. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L387

### What did you expect to happen?

I was expecting Pod#2 to be scheduled on another node because the scheduler should be aware of the previous, partially failed, retriable binding of Pod#1.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135854 (2 attempts case)

A test can follow these steps:

1. Create 2 nodes of same sizes
2. Create storage with WaitForFirstConsumer binding mode
3. Create pvc using dynamic binding (pvc#1), and a pod using the pvc (pod#1). The pod has preferred affinity for node#1 and takes up all of its resources.
3. Set up Bind plugin that will fail to bind pod#1 in the next cycle
4. Run scheduler
5. Expect: pvc#1 has selected-node annotation equal to node#1 (OK), pod#1 fails to bind (OK), pod#1 has nominated node name equal to node#1 (FAIL, nominated node name seems to be cleared)

To fully validate the scenario in the bug, add the following steps afterwards:

1. Tear down the scheduler
2. Add another pvc using dynamic binding (pvc#2) and a pod using that pvc (pod#2). The pod also has preferred affinity for node#1
3. Set up QueueSort plugin that will force pod#2 to be scheduled before pod#1
4. Run scheduler
5. Expect: pod#2 is scheduled on node#2 (FAIL, actual node#1), pod#1 is scheduled on node#1 (FAIL, unschedulable)

items.body:
### What happened?

When a CSI driver's `NodeStageVolume` returns `NOT_FOUND` (gRPC code 5), the kubelet continuously retries the operation with exponential backoff. However, the kubelet does not perform the recovery behavior specified in the CSI spec for this error code.

This results in pods being stuck in `ContainerCreating` state indefinitely, requiring manual intervention.

### What did you expect to happen?

According to the [CSI spec for NodeStageVolume errors](https://github.com/container-storage-interface/spec/blob/master/spec.md#nodestagevolume-errors), when `NOT_FOUND` is returned:

> **Condition:** Volume does not exist.
>
> **gRPC Code:** `5 NOT_FOUND`
>
> **Recovery Behavior:** "Caller MUST verify that the `volume_id` is correct and that the volume is accessible and has not been deleted before retrying with exponential back off."

The kubelet should follow this recovery behavior: **verify that the volume is accessible** before retrying.

Currently, the kubelet only retries `NodeStageVolume` without any verification step, which does not comply with the CSI spec.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy a CSI driver that returns `NOT_FOUND` from `NodeStageVolume` when the volume device is not present on the node
2. Create a PVC and a Pod that mounts it
3. Cause the volume to become inaccessible (e.g., detach via cloud API, node reboot, storage issue)
4. Observe:
   - Pod stuck in `ContainerCreating`
   - Kubelet retries `NodeStageVolume` indefinitely
   - No verification of volume accessibility as specified by CSI spec

### What happened?

We observed the e2e test `External Storage [Driver: disk.csi.azure.com] [Testpattern: Dynamic PV (default fs)] read-write-once-pod [MinimumKubeletVersion:1.27] should preempt lower priority pods using ReadWriteOncePod volumes` causes flakes in other e2e tests in a downstream CI job with Azure Disk CSI driver.

[The test](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4e94e70dcad423e9f59f12ac5a048d2137d20e86/test/e2e/storage/testsuites/readwriteoncepod.go#L133) runs a default (low-prio) pod1 with a `ReadWriteOncePod` volume and then starts a high prio pod2 that tries to use the same volume. What happened on a busy clusters, with all nodes at their attachment limit.

1. pod1 runs, pod2 is created.
2. The scheduler evicts pod1. That frees the RWOP volume and it also frees the last attachment slot on the node.
3. Some other e2e tests creates a Pod and scheduler puts it on the node, taking the last attachment slot.
4. The scheduler schedules pod2 agaian and it sees there is no node with a free attachment slot -> new round of eviction, now evicting a pod of unrelated e2e tests. The unrelated test will fail.  

We observed it with Azure, which can attach only 8 disks on the cheaper nodes, so it's more reproducible there.

The preemption test should not affect other e2e tests

items.title: PV Controller: workqueue accumulation when periodic resync overwhelms single-threaded volume and claim workers

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

labels.name: lifecycle/frozen

labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
**Problem**
The PersistentVolume controller periodically resyncs all volumes and claims to their workqueues, but [volumeWorker](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/volume/persistentvolume/pv_controller_base.go#L497) and [claimWorker](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/volume/persistentvolume/pv_controller_base.go#L555) are single-threaded. This can cause queue backlog when resync enqueues faster than workers consume.



**Root Cause**
In pv_controller_base.go [lines 324-326](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/volume/persistentvolume/pv_controller_base.go#L324-L326), the controller runs:

- A periodic `resync()` that enqueues all PVs and PVCs to their queues
- Single-threaded `volumeWorker` and `claimWorker` consuming from those queues

The `resync()` function enqueues all volumes and claims every `resyncPeriod`, which can add many items at once.







**Why Single-Threaded Processing is Required**
The code requires single-threaded processing because `syncVolume()` and `syncClaim()` access shared state that is not thread-safe:

1. `Local caches`: ctrl.volumes.store and ctrl.claims 
2. `Running operations map`: ctrl.runningOperations 
3. `Operation timestamps`: ctrl.operationTimestamps 


As noted in the code comments (lines 193-199 in pv_controller.go):
> "Every queue should have exactly one worker thread, especially syncClaim() is not reentrant. Two syncClaims could bind two different claims to the same volume or one claim to two volumes."
